fields_add.community: The Bank's own records put numbers to the resettlement. The appraisal estimated that land acquisition would leave over 10,000 project-affected persons entitled to compensation and more than 3,000 people needing relocation and livelihood restoration support; the appraisal document identified 685 project-affected persons in the four Maasai villages near the geothermal plants who were to be resettled because of air and noise pollution (World Bank completion report, 30 June 2018). The move to the resettlement site took place between 21 August and 2 September 2014. A census validation exercise in June 2013 cut the number of houses given as compensation for lost land and assets from 164 to 150, and the Inspection Panel recorded with concern that many of those ruled ineligible were widows, widowers, single mothers and one-person households, which it said lent credence to the complaint that 'the poor, orphans and widows' were excluded. Bank management told the Panel on 27 April 2015 that after validation 113 original project-affected heads of household, 22 households from polygamous families, one person with two structures and 13 natural-growth cases were awarded 149 houses in total; KenGen's compensation list named 126 heads of household receiving those 149 houses; and 179 heads of household were eventually compensated with a new house or cash. The Panel found serious inconsistencies between the documents it was given about affected people, even for the same census, and noted that the censuses and resettlement plans existed only in English, not in Maa, and that census-takers did not speak Maa and worked through translators. On the transmission lines, compensation for land stood at 90.9 per cent on the Kisii-Awendo line and 92.36 per cent on the 132kV Eldoret-Kitale line at closing, with KShs 63 million of unpaid compensation placed in an escrow account (World Bank completion report). Thirteen project-affected households were evicted at Ng'ati Farm in July 2013 and received government compensation; Bank management said the evictions were unrelated to the project.
fields_add.killed_note: The World Bank completion report records several community, occupational and vehicular safety incidents inside the Olkaria project site that resulted in fatalities between 2013 and 2015, without giving a number.
fields_add.confidence_note: The household and house counts, the relocation dates and the outstanding transmission-line compensation come from the World Bank's own Inspection Panel investigation report and completion report. The Panel itself reported that the documents it was given about affected people contained serious inconsistencies, so the counts should be read as what each document states rather than as a settled figure.

uganda-rdp3-road-compensation.title: Unpaid and late road compensation, Kampala-Gayaza-Zirobwe

uganda-rdp3-road-compensation.point: Gayaza town, Wakiso District, on the Kampala-Gayaza-Zirobwe road named in the resettlement completion report (OpenStreetMap town point)

lenders.name: World Bank (IDA)
lenders.role: Third Phase of the Road Development Program (P074079), credits IDA-39760 and IDA-H1220: SDR 45.970 million (US$67.60 million equivalent) and SDR 27.201 million (US$40.00 million equivalent). Original commitment XDR 73.17 million, of which XDR 72.84 million was disbursed. Approved 2 September 2004, effective 23 June 2005, restructured four times, closing extended from 31 December 2009 to 31 October 2011. Environmental category B. No co-financier. Quality of supervision was rated Moderately Unsatisfactory by the Independent Evaluation Group, which said evidence of compliance with the resettlement safeguard was insufficient and that compensation for many project-affected persons was pending (World Bank Implementation Completion and Results Report ICR2185, 17 May 2012; IEG ICR Review, 25 January 2013).

uganda-rdp3-road-compensation.community: The roads were built across land people were living and working on, and payment for it ran years late. The completion report states that the implementing agency, the Uganda National Roads Authority, 'did not handle, in a timely manner, cases of delayed compensation of project-affected persons, leading to delayed site handover', and that payment of compensation for properties 'has continued to cause project implementation problems'. The resettlement completion report for the Kampala-Gayaza-Zirobwe stretch, quoted by the Independent Evaluation Group, says: 'A number of complaints were raised and resolved to expedite acquisition of the right of way as the contractor was already on site. However, many complaints are still pending and are to be settled under injurious affection.' The Independent Evaluation Group concluded that evidence of compliance with the resettlement safeguard was insufficient and that compensation for many project-affected persons was pending, and said that given the significant number of project-affected persons the completion report should have given more detail from the resettlement completion reports and explained how pending compensation cases would be resolved. Neither Bank document gives a number for the people whose compensation was unpaid, or for the people moved.
uganda-rdp3-road-compensation.killed_note: No deaths are reported in the Bank documents for this project.
uganda-rdp3-road-compensation.displaced_note: ICIJ gives 4,925 for this project, which is its count of project-affected people and not a count of people moved. No World Bank document found for this project counts people actually relocated; the Independent Evaluation Group said the completion report should have provided that information and did not.
uganda-rdp3-road-compensation.outcome: The project closed on 31 October 2011 having upgraded or reconstructed 170 km of national roads. Compensation claims on the Kampala-Gayaza-Zirobwe section remained pending at the time of the resettlement completion report, to be settled under the Ugandan law of injurious affection. Overall Bank performance and overall borrower performance were both rated Moderately Satisfactory, with quality of supervision and implementing agency performance rated Moderately Unsatisfactory.

lenders.name: World Bank (IDA)
lenders.role: Emergency Multisector Rehabilitation and Reconstruction Project (P057296), credit and grants IDA-37030, IDA-H0100, IDA-H1930 and IDA-H3450: SDR 325.6 million credit (US$412 million equivalent), SDR 33.2 million initial grant (US$42 million), SDR 86.2 million first additional grant (US$125 million) and SDR 7.7 million second additional grant (US$12 million). Original commitment XDR 358.8 million, revised to XDR 451.1 million, with XDR 449.9 million disbursed. Approved 6 August 2002, closing 15 May 2010 after two extensions (World Bank Implementation Completion and Results Report ICR00001506, 29 October 2010).

lenders.name: World Bank (IDA), supplemental financing
lenders.role: The US$125 million supplemental financing carries project number P096305. The completion report says this first additional grant, SDR 86.2 million or US$125 million equivalent, was approved in November 2005 and became effective on 6 March 2006; the Bank's project record for P096305 gives a board approval date of 8 December 2005. Its stated purpose was to cover cost overruns, fill a financing gap in the original programme and extend the project to provinces that had been held by rebels.

drc-selembao-loange-compensation.community: Two sets of people lost assets or work to the Bank-financed works. At the Drève de Selembao in Kinshasa the site was occupied, and the completion report says a resettlement plan worth US$0.533 million was drawn up to pay 233 people for loss of land, dwellings, trees and crops; a figure of US$533,000 for a compensation plan covering the 'involuntary resettlement of 233 people' appears in the same report's results table. For the Loange bridge on road lots 6 and 7 of the Batshamba-Tshikapa road, the completion report says the pirogue operators who had been ferrying goods across the Loange river lost that work, and that a resettlement and compensation plan of about US$1 million was drawn up under the Bank's involuntary resettlement policy OP 4.12 and put in place before the crossing opened to traffic. The report gives no number for the pirogue operators. A separate compensation payment of US$527,707 is recorded for right of way and land acquisition under the electricity component. The documents do not say whether the people at Selembao or the Loange operators were paid in full.
drc-selembao-loange-compensation.killed_note: No deaths caused by the project are reported in the completion report. The report describes the wider war in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, including massive internal displacement and human rights abuses, as the background the project was built in, not as a project effect.
drc-selembao-loange-compensation.displaced_note: ICIJ gives 3,675 for this project, which is its count of project-affected people and not a count of people moved. The completion report records 233 people compensated for loss of land, dwellings, trees and crops at the Drève de Selembao under an involuntary resettlement plan, and gives no number for the pirogue operators at the Loange river.
drc-selembao-loange-compensation.outcome: The project closed on 15 May 2010. Construction of the Loange and Lovua bridges cut travel on the Kinshasa-Matadi route from eight days to about six hours, by the completion report's account. Two of the road contracts, lots 6 and 7, were terminated after the Bank found the contractor unable to do the work, and the contract was re-let to the next-ranked bidder. No follow-up report on the people compensated at Selembao or on the Loange pirogue operators was found.

lenders.name: World Bank (IDA)
lenders.role: Urban Water Project (P056256), credits and grants IDA-39620, IDA-H1320, IDA-H7660 and trust funds TF-11457 and TF-92093. Original commitment SDR 71 million (US$103 million equivalent), fully disbursed; revised to SDR 103.3 million (US$153 million equivalent), also fully disbursed. Approved 27 July 2004, effective 21 March 2005, restructured three times, closing extended from 31 December 2010 to 30 June 2016. Co-financiers: Nordic Development Fund and the Dutch Government. Implementing agency: Ghana Water Company Ltd. Outcome, Bank performance and borrower performance were all rated Moderately Unsatisfactory (World Bank Implementation Completion and Results Report ICR00003112, 21 December 2016).

companies.name: Ghana Water Company Limited (GWCL)
companies.role: State water utility and implementing agency. The completion report says it paid compensation to affected people out of its own funds so that works could go ahead when the government did not release the money, and that reimbursement from the government was still outstanding when the report was written.

ghana-urban-water-unpaid-compensation.conditions: A dated covenant added when the project was restructured required the borrower to set up an escrow account used only for compensation and disturbance allowances to project-affected persons. The completion report says the account was opened on time but was never funded on time, and lists the borrower's failure to pay full compensation costs as a major implementation issue.
ghana-urban-water-unpaid-compensation.community: Transmission and distribution pipes were laid through land and through places where people traded. At the time the completion report was drafted in December 2016, six months after the credit closed, 'compensation remains outstanding to about 4,100 PAPs who were temporarily disturbed during the laying of the transmission and distribution lines' under the Subsequent Year Investment Programme. The report says GHC 3,417,847.25 was needed for those payments, that the Ministry of Finance had not released the funds and that there was 'still no commitment by the government to resolve this issue'. Twenty sites were still unpaid, and the identification and confirmation of ownership of three more sites in Bawku and Navrongo was still going on. A further 39 project-affected persons under the First Year Investment Programme 'could not be traced for payment as they had moved their trades away from the pipe laying route'. The Bank raised the compensation problem with the water company and the Ministry of Finance on numerous occasions 'without timely resolution'. The Independent Evaluation Group's review states that the project 'closed with unresolved resettlement matters due to the government's lack of compliance'.
ghana-urban-water-unpaid-compensation.killed_note: No deaths are reported in the Bank documents for this project.
ghana-urban-water-unpaid-compensation.displaced_note: ICIJ gives 3,630 for this project, which is its count of project-affected people and not a count of people moved. The completion report counts people by compensation owed rather than by relocation: about 4,100 people temporarily disturbed and still unpaid, and 39 traders who could not be traced. No Bank document found for this project counts people physically relocated.
ghana-urban-water-unpaid-compensation.outcome: The credit closed on 30 June 2016. Six months later the compensation was still unpaid, with no government commitment to settle it, and the water company was still awaiting reimbursement for the compensation it had paid itself. The Independent Evaluation Group rated the project's outcome Moderately Unsatisfactory and drew the lesson that covenants on escrow accounts for resettlement compensation should bind the borrower not only to open the account but to keep it funded. No later document recording whether the about 4,100 people were eventually paid was found.

lenders.name: World Bank (IDA)
lenders.role: Burkina Faso Donsin Transport Infrastructure Project (P120960), credit IDA-52510: US$85 million approved 16 May 2013, signed 13 June 2013, effective 28 October 2013, US$79.65 million disbursed, 98 per cent of the credit. Closing was extended from 30 June 2018 to 30 April 2019. Environmental category A, triggering the Bank's policies on environmental assessment, physical cultural resources and involuntary resettlement. The credit financed the connector and rural roads to the planned new airport; the airport itself was not financed by it, and the Bank advised the government to run a separate resettlement plan for the airport (World Bank Implementation Status and Results Report ISR36770, archived 30 April 2019; Independent Evaluation Group ICR Review, 17 June 2020).

companies.name: Maîtrise d'Ouvrage de l'Aéroport de Donsin (MOAD)
companies.role: The Burkinabè public body running the Donsin airport works and the resettlement; it told the Bank's completion mission that all complaints had been cleared, including those over farmland for affected people.

burkina-donsin-airport-roads-resettlemen.community: People were moved off the land for the new airport and its roads, and the land paperwork was not finished. The Bank's last implementation report before closing states that 'Project Affected Persons (PAP) have been resettled and compensated accordingly' and that 'about 942 households living on the airport platform and 20 others for the access road were compensated'. It adds that 'while people have been resettled in newly constructed houses, the major issue remaining is the full compensation of lost agriculture land'. The Independent Evaluation Group's review repeats the figures of about 942 households near the future airport and 20 in the right of way of the access roads, and says that 'the process of delivering property titles has not been fully achieved and the Bank team was continuing to monitor the situation after project closure'. It records that the appraisal document counted 61 hectares of farmland involved and 327 mobile street vendor kiosks with potential claims, that the completion report gave no detail on either, and that the task team leader confirmed the street vendors did receive compensation. The appraisal document also listed 20 tombs and two patches of sacred trees to be relocated; the completion report does not say what happened to them and the Independent Evaluation Group noted that gap. Both Bank documents record a side effect for people nearby: land prices rose around the new airport area.
burkina-donsin-airport-roads-resettlemen.killed_note: No deaths are reported in the Bank documents for this project. The Bank team recorded that it was not informed of any case of gender-based violence during implementation.
burkina-donsin-airport-roads-resettlemen.displaced_label: households compensated near the airport site, of whom an unstated number were resettled in newly built houses
burkina-donsin-airport-roads-resettlemen.displaced_note: ICIJ gives 3,324 for this project, which is its count of project-affected people and not a count of people moved. The Bank's own figure is about 942 households living on the airport platform plus 20 households in the access-road right of way, all recorded as compensated, with people resettled in newly constructed houses. The documents do not break out how many of the 942 households were physically moved, and the airport platform itself was not financed by this credit.
burkina-donsin-airport-roads-resettlemen.outcome: The credit closed on 30 April 2019 with 98 per cent disbursed and the rehabilitation of 42.5 km of rural roads in the Donsin area completed. The implementation of social safeguards was rated satisfactory. The outstanding items at closing were the full compensation of lost agricultural land and the delivery of property titles, which the Bank team said it would keep monitoring after the project closed. A private partner to run the current and future Ouagadougou airport had not been selected when the project closed.

lenders_add.role: AFR RI-Regional Rusumo Falls Hydroelectric Project (P075941): IDA Credits 52950 and 52960, IDA Grants H8720 and H8730, and Nile Basin Initiative Grant TF-57297. The project closed with a Moderately Unsatisfactory safeguards performance rating because works at the resettlement village and the ferry ramp were unfinished, and a post-closure action plan was required (World Bank Implementation Completion and Results Report ICR00541, 9 December 2025).

sources_add.title: Rusumo falls dam construction project victims left stranded by water and food shortages (Ferdinand Mbonihankuye, supported by the Rainforest Journalism Fund and the Pulitzer Center)

fields_add.community: The World Bank completion report adds that the local area development programme built more than 40 schemes at a cost of more than US$13.8 million, that health and safety supervision of those works was in many cases poor and that two worker deaths occurred at one site. At closing, in all three countries some of the finished buildings, including courts, markets and health centres, were still not in use because no staff had been assigned to run them, and many lacked operation and maintenance plans, funding for running costs and connections to electricity or water. A completion audit of the livelihood restoration programme, the second of two independent standard of living surveys, found that more than 70 per cent of project-affected people reported improved livelihoods. The social specialist on the project's independent panel of environmental and social experts resigned in 2019 and was not replaced. Reporting from Burundi by Ferdinand Mbonihankuye, supported by the Rainforest Journalism Fund and the Pulitzer Center, followed the transmission lines that carry 26 MW from Rusumo Falls to the Gitega, Kobero and Muyinga stations in Burundi: 417 pylons were installed, and a NELSAP assessment cited in the article puts the area cleared for towers and substations at at least 24,081 hectares. The article reports that each household within a 15-metre radius of a pylon was compensated, and quotes people who said the money was too little to replace what they lost. Antoine Ndayisaba, a farmer in Mugutu village in Gitega province, said the 200,000 Burundian francs, about US$98, he received for a 15 by 15 metre pylon plot would not buy replacement land. The family of Antoine Kamwenubusa, a man in his sixties at the Ku Mazi urban centre in Nyabikere commune, Karusi province, refused the compensation and asked instead for plots the size of those they lost; a son said the family's banana plantations were decimated for the pylon work and the family's income fell. In Rwanda, Patricia Uwingabiye of Kirehe district said people in Nyankurazo used to grow sweet potatoes, beans and peas in the Rusumo marshes and can no longer reach those fields because of flooding from the Kagera River, and NELSAP's Gaspard Bikwemu put the loss of wooded savannah on Nyankurazo hill at about 10 hectares. In Tanzania, Jean Baraka Habonimana of Karagwe village said the water supply had got worse, and Rachid Mbaraka of Rusumo village said tap water was rationed to about once a week.
fields_add.ecosystem: The completion report states that site restoration and rehabilitation were appropriately and thoroughly addressed, and that the International Union for Conservation of Nature was engaged to prepare and support a vegetation and replanting plan.
fields_add.killed_note: The World Bank completion report records two worker deaths at one site of the local area development programme works, where it says the standard of health and safety supervision was in many cases poor.
fields_add.confidence_note: The two worker deaths, the unused buildings and the livelihood survey result are from the World Bank's own completion report. The Burundi transmission-line figures and the people quoted are from one named journalist's field reporting, supported by the Rainforest Journalism Fund and the Pulitzer Center, and have not been checked against a second source.

rwanda-rssp2-marshland-resettlement.place: Muvumba Perimeter 8 and Muvumba V marshlands, Nyagatare District, and marshlands in Gatsibo, Nyanza, Muhanga, Ngoma and Kirehe Districts, Rwanda
rwanda-rssp2-marshland-resettlement.point: Nyagatare town, Nyagatare District, the district holding the Muvumba Perimeter 8 and Muvumba V marshland schemes named in the resettlement completion report (OpenStreetMap town point)

lenders.name: World Bank (IDA)
lenders.role: Rwanda Second Rural Sector Support Project (P105176), IDA-H4080: SDR 21.30 million (US$35 million equivalent), approved 24 June 2008, closed 31 October 2012, fully disbursed at XDR 21.30 million. It financed gravity irrigation schemes in marshlands covering 3,324 hectares. The government of Rwanda financed all resettlement costs. The Bank's involuntary resettlement policy OP 4.12 and its policy on projects on international waterways OP 7.50 were triggered; riparian notifications were sent on 5 May 2008 (World Bank Implementation Completion and Results Report ICR2741, 30 April 2013).

rwanda-rssp2-marshland-resettlement.community: People farming and living in the marshlands lost crops, land, cattle sheds and houses. The resettlement implementation completion report for the project, prepared by the project's social safeguards team in July 2012 and disclosed by the Bank, states: 'The numbers of affected people due to the project activities in all the marshlands so far are 3,088 in total. These people had activities either in the marshlands where canals were constructed or in the areas to be flooded and some buildings (such as houses) were built in buffer zones. Therefore, the project had to construct 36 houses in total in terms of compensations.' The total paid in the resettlement process was Rwf 460,938,198. Twelve to thirteen resettlement action plans were prepared and carried out, for the Nyarubogo dam and irrigation channel, the Ntende-Rwagitima channel and dam, the Kiliba dam, the Rugeramigozi dam, the Kinyegenyege marshland, Gisaya, Kibaya, Kinyogo, Muvumba V, and the Muvumba VIII dam and channels. At Muvumba 8, cattle farms were flooded by the dam and the people affected were given cash to buy other farms for their animals; the report says most of them lived by animal keeping. Houses were replaced in three ways: new houses built in grouped settlements known as imidugudu, with the project providing materials and technical support and the work done as community labour; cash to renovate a house the household already owned elsewhere; or materials to finish an unfinished house. Cattle sheds were paid for in cash after valuation. The report's own list of grievances includes delays in payment for some affected people, caused by long district payment processes; people who did not find their names on the compensation lists in their sectors and were paid only after the lists were checked again; dissatisfaction with the value put on crops and assets; burial grounds that had not been declared at valuation, whose owners agreed to be helped to move them off the project sites; and family land conflicts, after families could not agree whose name went on the plan, which were sent to the local courts. The project's own conclusion is that all compensation was completed and that affected people were better off than before.
rwanda-rssp2-marshland-resettlement.killed_note: No deaths are reported in the Bank documents for this project.
rwanda-rssp2-marshland-resettlement.displaced_label: households for whom new houses were built as compensation
rwanda-rssp2-marshland-resettlement.displaced_note: ICIJ gives 3,088 for this project. That figure is, to the person, the total of affected people in the project's own resettlement implementation completion report, which counts everyone who had activities in the marshlands where canals were dug or in the areas to be flooded, plus people whose buildings stood in buffer zones. It is not a count of people moved. The same report says the project built 36 houses in total as compensation.
rwanda-rssp2-marshland-resettlement.outcome: The credit closed on 31 October 2012, fully disbursed. The marshland rehabilitation works were finished and affected people were given priority in the redistribution of plots in the rehabilitated marshlands; the resettlement report says they are now growing rice there. Some affected people were employed on the dam works at a minimum of Rwf 1,000 a day, and others at the cooperatives in the marshlands at about Rwf 700 a day. The project's resettlement report says compensation was 100 per cent complete at all sites. The Bank's completion report says the project surpassed the requirements of the involuntary resettlement policy and that districts provided land for land to farmers who had to be moved off government-owned marshlands.

sources.title: Rwanda - Rural Sector Support Project: Resettlement implementation completion report for RSSP2 (RP625 V16)
Rwanda - Second Rural Sector Support Project: Implementation Completion and Results Report (ICR2741)

rwanda-rssp2-marshland-resettlement.confidence_note: The counts of 3,088 affected people, 36 houses built and Rwf 460,938,198 paid, and the list of grievances including late payments and people missing from the compensation lists, all come from the project's own resettlement implementation completion report, disclosed by the World Bank. That report was written by the project's social safeguards team and reaches a wholly favourable conclusion about its own work, so its judgement that people are better off is the implementer's, not an independent finding. No independent field study of this resettlement was found. The Bank's completion report repeats the favourable assessment and adds no separate count.

lenders.name: World Bank (IDA)
lenders.role: Transport Sector Project (P102000), credit IDA-46000: US$225 million approved 30 June 2009, effective 12 November 2009, US$220,463,716 disbursed. Additional financing, credit IDA-55490: US$25 million, US$22,536,317 disbursed. Total project cost US$250 million at approval and US$243,000,033 disbursed. Closing was extended by 42 months in total, from 30 June 2015 to 31 December 2018, with a final six-month extension granted because of late payment of resettlement compensation on the Ayamfuri-Asawinso road works. Environmental category A. The overall safeguards rating was downgraded to Moderately Unsatisfactory in June 2013 because the Ministry of Finance had not released money for compensation payments (World Bank Implementation Completion and Results Report, 24 June 2019).

ghana-transport-ayanfuri-compensation.community: Payment for land and property taken for the road was held back for years. The completion report says that 'delays in paying resettlement compensation to Project Affected Persons (PAPs) during implementation severely curtailed some civil works', that work on the Ayamfuri-Asawinso corridor 'revealed several gaps in the identification of PAPs, leading to increased compensation', and that failure by the client to pay compensation on time cost the project about two years and US$15 million in contractor claims for idle time, which the government had still not settled. The overall safeguards rating was downgraded to Moderately Unsatisfactory in June 2013 because the Ministry of Finance had not released the money for compensatory payments to affected people. The Independent Evaluation Group's review says the main cause of the failure to pay on time was poor coordination between the Ghana Highway Authority and the Land Valuation Division, and that the underlying reason was a shortage of government funds for compensation. The appraisal classified the project category A partly because 87 households were to permanently lose their properties. Graves and burial sites lay inside the right of way of the Ayanfuri-Asawinso road; because there is no formal mechanism in Ghana for that situation, the implementing agency negotiated with local communities to meet traditional requirements for moving the remains of the dead out of the right of way. Slow responses to drainage problems during the works resulted in flooding. The Independent Evaluation Group states that details were not given in the completion report of how many people were finally relocated or how much they were paid.
ghana-transport-ayanfuri-compensation.killed_note: No deaths caused by the works are reported in the Bank documents. The completion report's figures on road deaths, which fell from 22 per 10,000 vehicles in 2009 to 9.74 in 2018, count road-traffic deaths across Ghana and are not deaths caused by the project.
ghana-transport-ayanfuri-compensation.displaced_note: ICIJ gives 2,862 for this project, which is its count of project-affected people and not a count of people moved. The appraisal figure of 87 households that were to permanently lose their properties is a plan figure. The Independent Evaluation Group states that the completion report did not say how many people were finally relocated or how much compensation was paid, and no Bank document found for this project gives that count.
ghana-transport-ayanfuri-compensation.outcome: The project closed on 31 December 2018, having rehabilitated the Ayanfuri-Asawinso road and built urban roads in the Accra East Corridor. Safeguards compliance was rated Moderately Satisfactory at closing, after the government resolved most of the outstanding concerns; the contractor's claim for idle time caused by the unpaid compensation was still unsettled. A resettlement plan audit was launched for this project and for the Abidjan-Lagos Transport and Transit Facilitation Project. The Independent Evaluation Group drew the lesson that compensation funds should be held in an escrow account until needed and that a national resettlement law would strengthen protection for affected people in Ghana.

ghana-transport-ayanfuri-compensation.confidence_note: The withheld compensation, the June 2013 safeguards downgrade, the two-year delay, the US$15 million in contractor idle-time claims and the moving of graves out of the right of way are all stated in the World Bank's own completion report and in the Independent Evaluation Group's review. What is thin is the count of people harmed: the Independent Evaluation Group says the completion report gave no figure for how many people were finally relocated or how much they were paid, the 87 households is an appraisal plan figure, and no independent field report on this road was found. The documents spell the road both Ayanfuri and Ayamfuri.

fields_add.community: The completion report's table of the Community Compensation and Reinstallation Programme covers sixteen places in the Belabo, Ngoura and Bétaré Oya districts, and records at seven of them that infrastructure was built but that other restoration actions and improvements to living standards 'were not provided': Ouami, Haman, Woumbou, Ndanga Gandima, Gberi, Bétaré Oya and Bodomo-Issa. At Bodomo-Issa the classrooms were 76 per cent complete and construction of the health unit had not started. At four more places, Goyoum, Petit Ngaoundéré, Garga Sarali and Ndokayo, some restoration and living-standard actions 'remain to be done'. Beside the 52 dwellings at Lom Pangar, the table lists 9 dwellings with 9 toilets and 9 kitchens at Lom II. Across 15 villages hit by the fall in the reservoir's water quality the programme built six classrooms, 42 latrine blocks, 35 water wells with hand pumps, 21 drying areas, two nursing homes, two community homes, two market sheds and two tracks. The report says the livelihood restoration programme for affected people was still at a starting phase at closing. The Inspection Panel's report on the two former workers' complaint sets out what happened on the construction site. The contractor employed more than 3,000 workers over the life of the project, up to 1,293 people at the August 2015 peak, 875 of them local; by December 2017 only 35 were left, 8 of them foreign. An on-site testing campaign in August 2014 found Hepatitis B in 67 of 500 workers; Bank management, citing the supervising engineer's progress reports, said 34 of them were treated free of charge at a hospital nearby and 33 left the site at the end of their contracts or resigned before being treated. The complainants said none of the 67 had been treated and that some were dismissed while others were pushed to leave. The complainants also said that the bonus the contractor paid 10 managerial employees instead of overtime was conditional on withdrawing all pending cases before the national courts, so they did not accept it as payment for the overtime; Bank management said the labour code is open to conflicting readings on whether managerial employees are owed overtime and that national courts would have to settle it. Workers also told the Panel that people found to have HIV/AIDS, tuberculosis or a hernia were dismissed from the site without support.
fields_add.killed_note: A World Bank supervision mission of 15 to 20 June 2013 recorded four worker deaths on the site, which it attributed to illness unrelated to the workers' tasks. The completion report also records three accidents downstream of the dam during project implementation, without giving casualties, and says that at closing there were still safety risks for people living beside the river and other users during rapid changes in flow rates.
fields_add.confidence_note: The places where restoration actions and improvements to living standards were not provided, and the worker figures on Hepatitis B, employment and the four 2013 deaths, come from the World Bank's own completion report and from the Inspection Panel's 2018 report. What the workers say and what Bank management says about the Hepatitis B cases and the overtime bonus do not agree, and the Panel did not resolve the difference: the Board accepted an action plan instead of an investigation.
